---
title: "Travel time as IV: first-stage collapse"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

## Motivation

Travel time to the nearest healthcare facility is a classical IV in maternal-health economics: in supply-constrained settings, it strongly predicts whether a mother reaches a facility for delivery, while plausibly affecting child outcomes only through the delivery decision itself.

Under the regime-shift hypothesis, travel time should be a *strong* first-stage instrument in the supply-constrained era (pre-2011) and a *weakening* one as the C-section trajectory becomes demand-driven. Visualizing the first-stage coefficient on travel time across waves is the most direct test of that claim.

## Data and setup

Travel-time-to-facility values come from the Malaria Atlas Project's accessibility raster, extracted per DHS cluster centroid (jittered at the standard DHS 5–10 km level for rural / 2 km for urban clusters). The first-stage regression — individual C-section status on log travel time, with controls — is estimated wave-by-wave.

Implementation: `scripts/30_spatial/34_spatial_models_bd.R`.

## Interpretation

The first-stage coefficient on log travel time declines (in absolute value) across waves. In 2004 the relationship is strong; by 2022 it is much weaker, consistent with the regime-shift account in Chapter 3.

Two readings are possible:

1. **Power loss.** The weakening relationship makes travel-time-based 2SLS estimation noisier in late waves. Even if exclusion held, the IV would be too weak in 2022 to identify the treatment effect with useful precision.

2. **Structural change.** The instrument's meaning is changing: in 2004 travel time captured access; by 2022 it captures something else (urban / rural living style, infrastructure, demand for elective procedures). The exclusion restriction's plausibility is therefore *time-dependent*.

Either reading reinforces Part II's conclusion: there is no single IV identification strategy that gives a coherent causal estimate across the full BDHS panel.
